raw_text: Natural Products Synthesis
Total Synthesis of Principinol B
Qiang Du, Zhibo Fan, and Ming Yang\*

Abstract: We have accomplished the first and asymmetric total synthesis of principinol B, a grayanoid possessing an oxabicyclo[3.2.1] architecture. A functionalized 5/7/6/5 tetracyclic intermediate was assembled in a convergent manner by a diastereoselective intermolecular aldol reaction and subsequent carbonyl–olefin metathesis of two enantiomerically enriched fragments. The oxabicyclo[3.2.1] architecture containing a 6,10-ether bridge was constructed by the Williamson ether synthesis.

Grayanoids are a large family of polycyclic natural products (> 300 members) isolated from the flowering plants of the genus Ericaceae.<sup>[1]</sup> They exhibit a wide range of biological activities, including sodium-channel-modulating, analgesic, anticancer, antiviral, antifeedant, insecticidal and bactericidal activities, and attract significant attention from synthetic chemists.<sup>[2–9]</sup> Originating from the ent-kaurane skeleton through a A-nor-B-homo rearrangement,<sup>[1]</sup> typical grayanoids possess a 5/7/6/5 tetracyclic carbon framework, and the central seven-membered carbon ring has become a signature feature of the family. To date, 18 total syntheses of grayanoids have been accomplished by seven research groups.<sup>[2–8]</sup> Several methods have been developed to construct the tricky seven-membered carbon ring,<sup>[10]</sup> such as photo-santonin rearrangement by the Matsumoto group<sup>[2]</sup> and Ding group,<sup>[5c]</sup> SmI -promoted intramolecular pinacol coupling by the Shirahama group,<sup>[3]</sup> SmI -promoted intramolecular reductive coupling of aldehyde and enone by the Newhouse group,<sup>[4]</sup> oxidative dearomatization-induced intramolecular Diels–Alder reaction<sup>[5a]</sup> and photo-Nazarov cyclization<sup>[5b]</sup> by the Ding group, bridgehead carbocationinduced Prins cyclization by the Luo group,<sup>[6]</sup> intramolecular vinylogous aldol reaction<sup>[7a]</sup> and lithium-halogen exchange/ intramolecular nucleophilic addition to aldehyde<sup>[7c]</sup> by our group, intramolecular Pauson–Khand reaction by the Jia group,<sup>[8]</sup> and Dieckmann condensation by the Williams group.<sup>[9f]</sup> Considering the diversity of stereogenic centers on the seven-membered carbon ring of grayanoids, new strategies are still in high demand to assemble the medium-sized ring with specific stereochemistry. Principinol B (1,

Scheme 1), isolated by Hou and co-workers in 2014,<sup>[11]</sup> is a structural representative in which the C5 configuration is opposite to that of typical grayanoids. Although a similar stereogenic center was pre-introduced in the A-ring fragment in our recent convergent and modular total syntheses of rhodomollins A and B, the C1 stereogenic center could not be established directly and concisely.<sup>[7c]</sup> Herein, we report the first and asymmetric total synthesis of principinol B by direct introduction of the C1 and C5 stereogenic centers and construction of the central seven-membered ring by carbonyl–olefin metathesis.

Disassembly of 3 at C5=C6 double bond led to ketone 4, and intramolecular carbonyl–olefin metathesis<sup>[12]</sup> of which was expected to forge the central seven-membered carbon ring. We then disconnected C1�C10 bond, projecting its formation through a diastereoselective intermolecular aldol reaction using cyclopentanone 5 (A ring fragment) and aldehyde 6 (D/E ring fragment). Inspired by Shirahama’s synthetic studies of bicyclo[3.2.1]octane moiety of grayanoids,<sup>[9c]</sup> we think that a radical cyclization reaction could potentially fashion the bicyclo[3.2.1] carbon skeleton of 6 from lactone 7. The lactone could be constructed by a Tamao-Fleming oxidation/lactonization sequence from 8,<sup>[13]</sup> which was traced back to the known enantio-enriched cyclohexenone 9 with a silane substituent.<sup>[14]</sup> In this design, the silicon-bonded stereogenic center is assumed to relay stereocontrol throughout the synthesis, though it would be eliminated prior to the key radical cyclization reaction.

As shown in Scheme 2, our synthesis started from known compound 9,<sup>[14]</sup> which was synthesized from 2-cyclohexenone by an optimized two-step synthetic route through a catalytic enantioselective silicon 1,4-addition<sup>[15]</sup> and a Mukaiyama dehydrogenation<sup>[16]</sup> (for details see Supporting Information). 1,4-Addition of 9 with $\mathrm { a l l y l M e } _ { 2 } \mathrm { S i C H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { M g C l }$ (10) and $\mathrm { C u I } { \cdot } 0 . 7 5 \mathrm { M e } _ { 2 } \mathrm { S }$ followed by trapping the resultant enolate with ethyl cyanoformate (CNCOOEt) afforded the intermediate β-ketoester. Further treatment of the β- ketoester with NaH and 2,3-dibromopropene generated 8 in 64 % yield over two steps. The more reactive dimethylallylsilyl group was then converted into primary alcohol through a two-step Tamao-Fleming oxidation, and the resulting alcohol was trapped by the ester group which delivered lactone 11 in 73% overall yield. Next, in anticipation of probing the projected radical cyclization, ketone 11 was transformed to allylic alcohol 7 in 53 % overall yield through oxidative silane elimination using CuCl as oxidant<sup>[17]</sup> followed by Luche reduction of the resulting enone. Pleasingly, when we treated 7 with n-Bu SnH and 2,2’-azobis(2-methylpropionitrile) (AIBN), the cyclization reaction proceeded smoothly to give the desired product. When we treated the cyclization product with trifluoromethanesulfonic acid (TfOH) in one pot, the exocyclic C=C double bond was partially isomerized to internal C=C double bond to provide 12 and 13 in 20% and 31 % yield, respectively. The former could be converted into the latter in 60% yield (71% brsm) through treatment with TfOH in dichloromethane $\mathrm { a t } - 4 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } .$ Protection of the hydroxyl group of 13 with tert-butyldimethylsilyl trifluoromethanesulfonate (TBSOTf) followed by reduction of the lactone to lactol by diisobutylaluminium hydride (DIBAL-H) in one pot afforded 14 in 87% yield. Treatment of 14 with vinylmagnesium bromide (vinylMgBr) enabled the ring opening of the lactol to generate aldehyde, and subsequent addition of vinyl group to occur onto the resultant aldehyde. After quenching the resulting alkoxides with acetic anhydride $( \mathrm { A c } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } )$ , the diacetates could be obtained in one pot. Treatment of the diacetates with Palladium catalyst under reduction conditions [HCOOH and triethylamine (Et N)] smoothly effected the reduction of allylic acetate to allyl group.<sup>[18]</sup> One-pot removal of another acetate with MeONa and MeOH delivered 15 in 76 % overall yield. The primary alcohol of 15 was then converted to aldehyde by Parikh– Doering oxidation, providing the D/E-ring fragment 6 in 93 % yield.

With the D/E-ring fragment in hand, we turned our attention to construction of the tetracyclic carbon skeleton of 1. Aldol reaction between ketone 5 and aldehyde 6 afforded ketone 4 following TMS-protection of the newly formed secondary alcohol. The configuration of aldol product deTMS-4 was unambiguously confirmed by X-ray crystallographic analysis.<sup>[19]</sup> Next, we entered the stage of the planned carbonyl–olefin metathesis to assemble the central seven-membered carbon ring. Pleasingly, the initially attempted Petasis reagent provided desired cyclization product at 90°C with low yield. Further investigation indicated that freshly prepared Petasis reagent gave best result at 100 °C in toluene. After removal of TMS in one pot, tetracyclic compound 3 was obtained in 51% yield. Although Tebbe reagent generated the same active intermediate as Petasis reagent under basic conditions, it only caused decomposition of 4. The reason might be the Lewis acidity of Tebbe reagent and the instability of 4.

Given that Petasis reagent serves as not only an olefination reagent<sup>[20]</sup> but also a catalyst for olefin metathesis reaction,<sup>[21]</sup> the essence of this ring-closing reaction might also be a tandem carbonyl olefination/ring-closing meta thesis (RCM) sequence. As shown in Scheme 3, two substrates 20 and 22 were chosen for control reaction, which were synthesized from 4 by reduction of terminal alkene and methyl addition/elimination sequence, respectively, in order to investigate reaction mechanisms. Upon treatment of 20 with Petasis reagent in toluene at $1 0 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } ,$ the olefination product 21 was afforded in only 24% yield that was much lower than that for the cyclization product. However, when 22 was subjected to the standard ring-closing conditions (Petasis reagent, toluene, $1 0 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } )$ , no desired cyclization product was obtained, and only decomposition products were observed. It should be noted that RCM reaction of 22 with Grubbs catalysts also failed. These results indicated that the ring-closing reaction was not an olefination/RCM sequence. The carbonyl–olefin metathesis mechanism was then proposed as following: [2+2] cycloaddition of alkene 4 and titanacene carbene generated in situ from Petasis reagent delivered intermediate 24, retro-[2+2] cycloaddition of 24 followed by intramolecular [2+2] cycloaddition with carbonyl group provided intermediate 25, a subsequent retro-[2+2] cycloaddition of 25 culminated in desired tetracyclic compound 3 and $\mathrm { C p } _ { 2 } \mathrm { T i } { = } \mathrm { O }$

raw_text: From here, tetracycle 3 was converted into triene 16 over 3 steps by Dess–Martin oxidation of secondary alcohol to ketone, methyl cerium reagent addition onto the newly formed carbonyl group followed by tertiary alcohol elimination (Scheme 2). Unfortunately, attempted selective dihy droxylation of the C5=C6 double bond did not deliver the desired 1,2-diols. Further investigation indicated that C15=C16 double bond was the most reactive one in oxidation reaction, and C10=C20 double bond was the most unreactive one. Based on these results, C15=C16 double bond was first converted into epoxide in 77% yield through treatment of 16 with 3-chloroperoxybenzoic acid (m-CPBA) in dichloromethane at $- 6 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ . Dihydroxylation of 17 at C5=C6 double bond with $\mathrm { O s O _ { 4 } }$ followed by selective mesylation of the secondary alcohol afforded 18 in 65% yield over two steps. Different from our previous total syntheses of rhodomollins A and $\mathrm { B } , ^ { \mathrm { [ 7 c ] } }$ the transformation of the 1,2-diols to cyclic sulfonate failed on the dihydroxylation product of 17. To install the oxabicyclo[3.2.1] core structure, we set to introduce a tertiary hydroxyl group at the C10 position. Surprisingly, Mukaiyama hydration<sup>[22]</sup> of 18 provided pentacycle 19 instead of tertiary alcohol. It seemed that the $\mathrm { S } _ { \mathrm { N } } 2$ substitution of the Williamson ether synthesis on this substrate was a spontaneous reaction, which was also different from our previous experience.<sup>[7c]</sup>

Now, we entered the final stage of the total synthesis, and the epoxide should be reduced to alkene. However, the reduction of the epoxide with low-valent titanium $( \mathrm { I I I } ) ^ { [ 2 3 ] }$ prepared in situ from Cp TiCl and zinc powder only afforded allylic alcohol instead of alkene (for details see Supporting Information). The reason might be the hin drance of concave face of the bridged bicyclic ring system. To overcome the steric effects, less hindrance low-valent titanium generated from $\mathrm { T i C l } _ { 4 }$ and zinc powder was tested. To our delight, trace amount of desired alkene was observed. When pyridine was added into the reaction as a buffer, the yield of alkene improved significantly. After deprotection of both TBS with 6 M aqueous HCl in one pot, principinol B (1) was obtained in 66% yield.

We also tried other method, such as intramolecular ring opening of epoxide with tertiary alcohol, to construct the oxabicyclo[3.2.1] core structure of 1. As shown in Scheme 4, triene 16 was converted into bis-epoxide 26 in 60 % yield with excess of m-CPBA at $- 1 5 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } .$ . The structure of 26 was unambiguously confirmed by X-ray crystallographic analysis.<sup>[19]</sup> Mukaiyama hydration of 26 to introduce the tertiary alcohol delivered 27 in 74 % yield (dr=5 :4). However, 27 was not stable, and the ring-opening of epoxide failed with various conditions.

In conclusion, we have accomplished the first and asymmetric total synthesis of principinol B through convergent and modular synthetic strategies. An initially introduced removable silyl moiety carrying information of chirality effected stereocontrol in the synthesis. The bridged D/E ring fragment, which constitutes a bicycle[3.2.1]octane framework, was constructed through a radical cyclization. The 5/7/6/5 pentacyclic carbon skeleton was assembled by a diastereoselective intermolecular aldol reaction/carbonyl– olefin metathesis sequence. The ether ring of the oxabicyclo-[3.2.1] core structure was closed by the Williamson ether synthesis. This synthesis expands the strategies for the construction of the tricky seven-membered carbon ring, and will provide further inspiration for similar events in other contexts.
